lead: A blockchain stores history as blocks in a line. Each block has a header and a body. The header carries a pointer to the previous block, so blocks form an append-only chain. The body carries transactions. A block is created by a miner, checked by nodes, then added. This structure is used in Bitcoin, Ethereum and enterprise ledgers to make history easy to verify and hard to rewrite. This chapter shows the layers, the fields of a block, and why one edited transaction breaks later blocks.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2 on distributed ledgers and Chapter 5 on chain types.

blocks.text: Think of blockchain as four layers stacked. The application layer is what users touch: wallets, supply-chain forms, token dashboards. It creates transactions and reads confirmed state. The consensus layer decides which candidate block becomes next. It holds rules such as proof of work or voting, and the reward rules. The network layer moves transactions and blocks between peers. It uses peer-to-peer links, gossip and block propagation. The data layer is the ledger itself: blocks, headers, transactions, hash pointers and state. The data layer is the part this chapter opens. The layers are logical, not separate machines; one node runs all four. A wallet may run only the application layer and ask a node for data. Some syllabi call this overview and structure of a block.

sections.h3: Inside one block: header and body

blocks.text: A block is two parts. The header is metadata. The body is the transaction count and the transaction list. Header fields are:

items: version: the protocol rules the block follows.
previous block hash: the hash of the parent header, used as a pointer.
Merkle root: one hash that summarises every transaction in the body.
timestamp: the miner's claimed creation time, within protocol limits.
difficulty or target: the mining hardness, or the target value the header hash must beat.
nonce: a counter the miner changes to get a header hash below the target.

blocks.where: H<sub>n</sub> is the hash of block n; header<sub>n</sub> contains the previous block hash H<sub>n-1</sub>, the Merkle root, the timestamp, the target and the nonce; Hash is the chain's hash function, such as SHA-256 in Bitcoin.

blocks.text: The block hash is not Hash(transactions). It is Hash(header). The Merkle root is how the transactions enter the header. Unit 2 builds the Merkle tree. A candidate block is a block a miner has assembled but not yet accepted; it may still lack a valid nonce. The genesis block is block 0. It has no parent. Block height is the number of blocks before a block; the genesis block has height 0.

Each block stores the hash of the block before it. That value is a hash pointer: it points to the parent and also checks the parent's contents. Block 20 has previous hash 0000a1. Block 21 is mined with the hash of Block 20 as its previous hash. If Tx 2 inside Block 20 is edited, the body changes. The Merkle root must change from 7c2e to a new value. The header of Block 20 changes, so its hash changes. Block 21 still stores the old hash of Block 20, so its previous-hash field is now wrong. Block 21's header hash changes too, and every later block is affected.

For the chain to accept the edit, a miner must re-mine Block 20: find a new nonce so Hash(header) meets the target. Then re-mine Block 21 and all later blocks with the new previous hashes. Honest nodes reject the edited chain unless it wins under the consensus rule. In proof of work that usually means more total work than the honest chain. Appending a new block is cheap; rewriting old history is expensive. See Unit 3 for forks and consensus.

figure.caption: Editing Tx 2 changes the Merkle root from 7c2e to 7d5f, so Block 20 must be re-mined and Block 21's stored previous hash no longer matches. Block 21 and every later block must be re-mined, and the edited chain is accepted only if it wins under the consensus rule.

examples.question: Block 20 has previous hash 0000a1, Merkle root 7c2e, nonce 18, and 3 transactions. Block 21 is mined with the hash of Block 20 as its previous hash. Tx 2 in Block 20 is edited. Which fields of Block 20 and Block 21 change, and what must happen for the chain to accept the edit?
steps: Block 20 header: previous hash 0000a1, Merkle root 7c2e, nonce 18, timestamp and version. Body: Tx 1, Tx 2, Tx 3.
Edit Tx 2. The body of Block 20 changes. The transaction count stays 3. The Merkle root must change from 7c2e to a new value, for example 7d5f.
Hash of Block 20 = Hash(header). The header now has the new Merkle root, so the old hash of Block 20 is invalid. A new nonce must be found by mining.
Block 21 stores the old hash of Block 20 as its previous hash. That field must change to the new hash of Block 20. Block 21's header then changes, so Block 21 must be re-mined with a new nonce.

Every later block stores the old hash of its parent, so all later blocks must be re-mined too. The edited chain is accepted only if it wins under the consensus rule, for example by having more total work in proof of work.
examples.answer: Block 20 changes in Tx 2, Merkle root, nonce after re-mining, and block hash. Block 21 and all later blocks change in previous hash, nonce after re-mining, and block hash. The chain accepts the edit only if the edited chain is re-mined from Block 20 onward and wins under the consensus rule.

traps: Saying the block hash is the hash of the transactions only. It is Hash(header), and the Merkle root carries the transactions into the header.
Calling block height the number of transactions. Height is the count of blocks before this block; the genesis block has height 0.
Thinking the previous block hash is stored in the body. It is a header field.
Mixing the Merkle root with the block hash. The root summarises transactions; the block hash covers the whole header.
Assuming an edited old block can be accepted after changing only one field. Every later block stores the old hash, so later headers must be rebuilt.

quiz.q: Name four fields of a block header.
quiz.a: Any four of: version, previous block hash, Merkle root, timestamp, difficulty or target, nonce.

quiz.q: Why does the transaction list affect the header hash even though the body is not hashed directly?
quiz.a: The transactions are summarised by the Merkle root. The Merkle root is a header field. Changing a transaction changes the root, and the header hash covers the root.

quiz.q: Block 30 has previous hash 00ff, Merkle root ab12, and nonce 7. A transaction in Block 30 is changed. Which stored fields in Block 30 and Block 31 are now wrong?
quiz.a: In Block 30: the Merkle root ab12 is wrong, so Block 30's header and block hash are wrong; the nonce 7 may no longer meet the target. Block 30's own previous hash 00ff stays valid. In Block 31: the previous-hash field (the old hash of Block 30's header) is wrong, so Block 31's header and block hash are also wrong.

quiz.q: A node sees chain A with height 20 and chain B with height 19 but more total work. Under proof of work with the most-total-work rule, which chain is accepted? Explain in one line.
quiz.a: Chain B, because the rule compares total work, not height. A shorter chain can carry more work if its blocks used a harder target.
The first block of a blockchain, with height 0 and no previous block.

quiz.q: A header has version 1, previous hash 0000a1, Merkle root 7c2e, and nonce 18. Tx 2 is edited. Which of these four header values is directly determined by the transactions, and so becomes invalid when Tx 2 is edited?
quiz.a: The Merkle root 7c2e; the nonce is re-mined afterwards to make the new header hash valid.

quiz.q: Why is appending a new block cheaper than rewriting an old block?
quiz.a: Appending needs one new valid header and one new nonce. Rewriting an old block changes its hash and forces every later block to be re-mined, which costs work at every height.
A block a miner has assembled from a previous block and a set of transactions, before it is accepted by the network. It may still need a valid nonce.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry systems use the same header-first design for light clients: a phone can download headers and check proof of inclusion without storing every transaction. Rollups and modular chains separate data storage from execution, but they still publish roots and headers. Block explorers show height, previous hash, Merkle root and nonce for every block. Search next for block header fields, Merkle root, light client and header-first sync.
